For decimal fractions, the place values we work with are $\frac{1}{10}, \frac{1}{100}, \frac{1}{1,000}$ and $\frac{1}{10,000}$. They are called **tenths**, **hundredths**, **thousandths** and **ten thousandths**.

These place values are represented from biggest to smallest, moving to the right after the decimal point:

$$
\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|}
  \hline
    \text{units} & \text{.} & \text{tenths} & \text{hundredths} & \text{thousandths} & \text{ten thousandths} \\
    (1) & \text{.} & \left( \frac{1}{10} \right) & \left( \frac{1}{100} \right) & \left( \frac{1}{1,000} \right) & \left( \frac{1}{10,000} \right) \\
    \text{u} & \text{.} & \text{t} & \text{h} & \text{th} & \text{tth} \\
    \hline
    \end{array}
$$

The fractions for these place values are written in this way:

- 0.1 means zero units and one $\frac{1}{10}$
- 0.01 means zero units, zero tenths and one $\frac{1}{100}$
- 0.001 means zero units, zero tenths, zero hundredths and one $\frac{1}{1,000}$
- 0.0001 means zero units, zero tenths, zero hundredths, zero thousandths and one $\frac{1}{10,000}$.

As for whole numbers, we move to a new place value each time we reach 10. For example, this block of squares is divided into 100 parts.

One hundredth, which is $\frac{1}{100}$, may be shown like this:

![](https://electricbookworks.github.io/siyavula-open-textbooks-images/items/images/web/ebw-jss1-01-001.png)

Four parts of this block of 100 squares, which is $4\times \frac{1}{100}= \frac{4}{100}$, may be shown like this:

![](https://electricbookworks.github.io/siyavula-open-textbooks-images/items/images/web/ebw-jss1-01-002.png)

Ten parts of $\frac{1}{100}$, in other words, $10\times\frac{1}{100}$, may be shown like this:

![](https://electricbookworks.github.io/siyavula-open-textbooks-images/items/images/web/ebw-jss1-01-003.png)

There are 10 vertical columns in the block of squares. If 1 column out of 10 is shown in colour, we can write this as $\frac{1}{10}$. Therefore, 10 parts of $\frac{1}{100}$ is the same as $\frac{1}{10}$.

Similarly:

- 10 parts of $\frac{1}{1,000}$ is the same as $\frac{1}{100}$
- 10 parts of $\frac{1}{10,000}$ is the same as $\frac{1}{1,000}$.

records.raw_html:
Worked example 1.2: Finding place value in decimal numbers

Write down the place values of all the non-zero digits in the following number: 73,025.048

  1. Step 1: Write the number in a place value table. Show the decimal point clearly in your table.

  2. Step 2: Multiply each non-zero digit by the value of the column it is in.
records.prompt_text: Write down the place values of all the non-zero digits in the following number: 73,025.048
records.answer_text:
Step 1: Write the number in a place value table. Show the decimal point clearly in your table.

$$
\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|}
 \hline
 \text{tth} & \text{th} & \text{h} & \text{t} & \text{u} & \text{.} & \text{t} & \text{h} & \text{th} & \text{tth} \\
 (10,000) & (1,000) & (100) & (10) & (1) & \text{.} & (0.1) & (0.01) & (0.001) & (0.0001) \\
 \hline
 7 & 3 & 0 & 2 & 5 & . & 0 & 4 & 8 \\
 \hline
 \end{array}
$$

Step 2: Multiply each non-zero digit by the value of the column it is in.

$7\times10,000=70,000$\
$3\times1,000=3,000$\
$2\times10=20$\
$5\times1=5$\
$4\times 0.01=0.04$\
$8\times 0.001=0.008$
